Clovis. Around 466 to 511, he was the first king of the Franks, the man who conquered most of Roman Gaul and established the Frankish kingdom that would become France. His conversion to Catholic Christianity transformed him into the founder of both a realm and a Christian power.

Reigning from around 481 to 511, Clovis expanded Frankish territory from the lower Rhine all the way to the Pyrenees, consolidating his power over most of what is now France. His conversion to Catholicism was pivotal. According to legend, his wife Clotilda convinced him to invoke Christ during the Battle of Tolbiac around 496, and the victory that followed sealed his embrace of the faith. This Christianization made him an ally of the Roman ecclesiastical establishment and gave his rule divine sanction in the eyes of the Church.

Clovis proved ruthless in his military ambitions. He defeated the Visigoths at the Battle of Vouille in 507, eliminating a competing Germanic kingdom and extending Frankish dominion nearly to Spain's borders. He then established his capital at Paris, transforming it from a minor Roman city into the seat of Frankish power and a symbol of Christian kingship. His rise to power came at a cost. He murdered several of his own sons and kinsmen to consolidate his throne, a pattern of ruthlessness that would become common among his Merovingian heirs.

His reign marked the end of Roman Gaul and the beginning of a Germanic-Christian kingdom that would eventually become medieval France. He was the ancestor of Charlemagne, though separated by centuries and many generations of rule.
